The post A missing opportunity in the higher education transformation debate appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
Join HEPI, AHEP and TechnologyOne for a webinar on Thursday 12 November, 12pm-1pm, exploring the findings of The invisible majority (HEPI Report 205), a study of the professional and support staff who make up more than half of the UK higher education workforce. The session will examine the impact of financial pressures and organisational change on these staff, and discuss how universities can protect the skills and capability they depend on while budgets remain tight. Find details of speakers and register here.

This blog was kindly authored by Faye-Marie Adams, Compliance Officer, Robert Gordon University. She is writing in a personal capacity and the views expressed are her own.

Before launching major transformation programmes, institutions should create dedicated opportunities for staff to examine workflows across organisational boundaries. Process mapping, cross-functional improvement workshops and structured organisational learning activities should be treated as core components of transformation programmes rather than optional extras. The modest investment required may prevent considerably larger costs later when organisations discover they have solved the wrong problem.

Higher education providers are investing significant time and money in transformation. Across the sector, discussions focus on operating models, organisational structures and financial sustainability. These are important conversations. Yet they often overlook improving ways of working as a source of value. This may sound like an operational detail, but it is one of the biggest blind spots in current transformation debates.

While institutions understandably focus on future-state design, transformation ultimately succeeds or fails where new systems meet old processes, where strategic ambitions meet practical constraints and where change programmes meet the people expected to deliver them.

Staff continue to support students, answer enquiries, process transactions, maintain compliance and keep services running while adapting to new systems, structures and ways of working. The benefits of transformation are ultimately realised – or lost – through their experience of it.

This matters at a time when the sector is seeking greater efficiency and productivity. There is a risk in assuming technology alone will unlock transformational gains. Jisc’s 2024/25 Digital Experience Insights survey for higher education teaching staff highlights that while digital technologies are firmly embedded, persistent challenges and inconsistent support remain a reality for staff who are calling for clearer guidance, streamlined systems and dedicated development time.

My perspective on this comes not only from higher education, but from previous work in policing and healthcare transformation.

During the formation of Police Scotland, I led the implementation of the new HR shared services model across North Scotland. Bringing together teams, processes, policies and employment arrangements inherited from the former Tayside, Grampian and Northern police force areas was not simply an exercise in organisational redesign. It required people from different locations, functions and professional backgrounds to develop a shared understanding of how work was carried out and how it could be improved within a new national organisation.

A similar lesson emerged several years later while leading a Healthcare Improvement Scotland quality improvement project in a GP practice in Aberdeen.

Initial assumptions suggested administrative staff needed to absorb additional responsibilities. However, examining workflows, bottlenecks and staff experiences revealed a different picture: delays from pharmaceutical queries and medication-related issues. The eventual solution – recruiting a pharmacist – only became clear once the operating experience itself was understood. More importantly, the process created a shared understanding, challenged assumptions and shifted conversations from blame towards collaboration.

This pattern is not unique to policing or healthcare. Autonomy’s The Results are in: The UK’s Four-Day Week Pilot found that across sectors, organisations did not simply compress the same work into fewer hours; successful implementation involved rethinking how work was organised and delivered and adapting working practices to make reduced hours sustainable.

These experiences reinforce that meaningful transformation depends on understanding and reshaping work as it is actually done. The same lesson applies in higher education, where many of the most difficult challenges span organisational boundaries. Schools, Faculties and Professional Services departments collectively hold expertise spanning teaching, research, student support, technology, governance, finance, regulation, resources and risk. The challenge is not a lack of knowledge, but creating the capacity and conditions before transformation initiatives are launched.

This can appear inefficient. Workshops take time. Process mapping takes time. Building trust takes time. Yet the absence of shared understanding is often what proves costly. Organisations risk solving the wrong problem, implementing the wrong solution or simply transferring pressure from one part of the institution to another. That is why organisational learning deserves a more prominent place in discussions about transformation.

Across higher education, it is staff who keep institutions running while transformation programmes are delivered. They manage competing priorities, resolve unexpected problems and maintain business-as-usual amidst constant change. Their experience of how work happens in practice represents one of the sector’s most valuable – and often least utilised – sources of insight.

Improving working lives should not be viewed as an ancillary benefit of transformation. It is integral to organisational performance. As HEPI’s report Pressure Vessels: The epidemic of poor mental health among higher education staff highlights the pressures experienced by higher education staff have implications for both individuals and institutions. By removing and reducing excessive workloads, duplication and avoidable friction, institutions can release capacity and enable staff to focus their time, energy and expertise where they add greatest value. The benefits are not simply operational. They strengthen services and create greater capacity to support students and colleagues.

Institutions already devote considerable attention to transforming what they deliver. The next major efficiency gain is not hidden in a new technology platform or organisational chart, but in improving the operational realities of the people doing the work. In an increasingly competitive and pressurised environment, that may be one of the most important foundations for long-term sustainability and maintaining the student experience on which institutions ultimately depend.

title: WEEKEND READING: Research may lose money. Cutting it could lose universities even more
summary:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor Tim Jay, Associate Pro-Vice-Chancelor for Research and Knowedge Exchange, Professor Martin Jensen, Professor in Economics and Paula Gurteen, Head of Research and Knowledge Exchange, Faculty of Social Sciences, all of the University of Nottingham. There is an obvious response when an activity does not cover its costs: do […]

The post WEEKEND READING: Research may lose money. Cutting it could lose universities even more appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor Tim Jay, Associate Pro-Vice-Chancelor for Research and Knowedge Exchange, Professor Martin Jensen, Professor in Economics and Paula Gurteen, Head of Research and Knowledge Exchange, Faculty of Social Sciences, all of the University of Nottingham.

There is an obvious response when an activity does not cover its costs: do less of it. For UK universities under acute financial pressure, research increasingly appears to fit that description.

UKRI’s data pack on the financial sustainability of research puts the sector-wide research deficit at £6.18bn in 2023-24, up from £5.62bn the previous year. Only 66.6 per cent of the full economic cost of research was recovered, down from 69.3 per cent. The main source that universities draw on to subsidise the costs of research is non-publicly-funded teaching – primarily international student fees. The Office for Students’ latest assessment agrees; although financial sustainability across the higher education sector improved modestly in 2024–25, much of the improvement came from tuition-fee income, and forecasts of future recovery remain heavily dependent on international student recruitment growth.

That subsidy model is now under strain from both directions. Research costs are not being met, while international recruitment has become more volatile. Chris Husbands’ recent HEPI report describes structural underfunding of research, domestic teaching pressures and international volatility as three worsening elements of the same financial problem. Meanwhile, Universities UK and ARMA report that 19 per cent of surveyed universities have already reduced some academic research activity, while 79 per cent were considering doing so in future.

So research portfolios must be scrutinised. But the usual financial lens – grant income, overhead recovery and direct cost – captures only part of research’s institutional value. If research quality contributes to reputation and student demand, a cut that improves a faculty’s short-term cost position may weaken the income base of the wider university. The crucial complication that we present here is that this relationship may not look the same in every discipline.

Different disciplines speak differently to the market

Our analysis of Nottingham and 15 comparator research-intensive universities1 examined five broad disciplinary clusters: engineering, medicine and health, science, social sciences, and arts and humanities. We compared two dimensions of research performance – external research income and publication quality, measured through REF 2021 output GPA – with international undergraduate and postgraduate recruitment, measured as numbers of registrations. The results identify associations, not causal effects, but the patterns in the data are striking.

In engineering and medicine and health, international student recruitment is most strongly associated with the scale of external research income – in engineering, for example, the correlation between external research income and international PGT registrations is .76, while the correlation between REF output GPA and international PGTs is only .04. Within these discipline clusters, the scale of externally funded research may yield more visible signals of high-quality facilities, industrial connections, scientific activity and institutional capacity, which act as a draw for international students.

The social sciences work differently. International postgraduate recruitment is strongly associated with REF output quality, with a correlation of .70, but much less strongly with external research income, with a correlation of .33. A broadly similar disciplinary contrast appears for international undergraduate recruitment: REF-assessed output quality remains particularly important in social sciences, while research-income strength is more prominent in several other disciplinary clusters.

When we look at QS academic reputation data, the same broad pattern appears – in engineering and in medicine and health, QS academic reputation is more closely aligned with external research income. In the social sciences, it is more closely aligned with REF output GPA. This relationship with QS academic reputation may help explain some of the association between research metrics and international student recruitment, as we know that international students attend to QS rankings. Our analysis cannot establish the direction of causation or isolate the precise mechanism. However, the alignment with QS academic reputation reinforces the conclusion that research, reputation and international student recruitment should be treated as an interconnected system rather than assessed independently.

The other clusters – science, and arts and humanities – do not appear to follow simple rules. In science, publication quality and research income are more highly correlated than in other areas – the correlation between REF Output GPA and log research income is 0.58 in science disciplines while it is 0.14 and 0.21 in engineering and social sciences, respectively. In arts and humanities, research income appears to capture the scale and visibility of internationally recruitable portfolios such as media, communications and creative disciplines, but, in other arts disciplines, the relationship between research income and international student recruitment is less strong. But again, the details of the differences do not affect the central message here, that any single institutional proxy for research value will likely misread and misvalue important parts of the portfolio.

The danger of cutting what the accounts cannot see

For social sciences, our analysis suggests that publication excellence may therefore have a commercial value to universities that conventional models do not show. Our modelling of 16 research-intensive universities illustrates the potential scale. Moving one place up the social sciences rankings by REF output GPA is associated with around £13m more annual gross international fee income across postgraduate and undergraduate. This is not a forecast or proof that a REF improvement causes recruitment: the estimate is modelled from a small comparator group and will differ by institution. But the correlation is large enough to demand consideration in strategic decisions.

A narrow assessment might classify a social science unit with modest grant income as less valuable than a laboratory-based unit with a large external portfolio. Yet if publication quality sustains subject reputation, and subject reputation supports international student demand, reducing research time or critical mass in that unit may damage one of the key income streams being used to underpin the financial sustainability of the institution.

The effects will not be immediate. Reputation accumulates slowly, international recruitment responds with a lag, and the damage may become visible only after staff have left, doctoral communities have thinned and publication pipelines have weakened. By then, rebuilding capability is expensive and uncertain. Short-term savings may create a long-term revenue risk.

From one research model to a portfolio of models

Universities cannot conclude that every existing area of research must be protected. The sustainability gap is real, and selectivity is unavoidable. But the implication of the analyses we have shared here is that institutions need to consider different business models for research activity in different parts of the university.

In some disciplines, external research income, cost recovery, infrastructure utilisation and partnership scale will be central to the model. In others – especially social sciences, based on our modelling – publication quality, academic reputation, and international student recruitment should be treated as connected components of value. The House of Commons Education Committee has similarly concluded that financial pressures, research funding and international recruitment are inextricably connected, and that uncoordinated institutional decisions risk decline.

This points to three practical recommendations for universities. First, governing bodies should require research portfolio decisions to include downstream recruitment and reputation risks, not only immediate savings. Second, finance, research and student recruitment data should be brought together at discipline level; university-wide averages conceal the relationships leaders need to understand. Third, proposed reductions should be stress-tested over several recruitment cycles.

The sector cannot cross-subsidise research indefinitely on its current terms, and government and funders still need to address the underlying failure of cost recovery. But universities should avoid treating all research as the same kind of financial problem. In social sciences, cutting research quality may not merely reduce an institutional cost. It may also erode the reputation that attracts international students and, with it, part of the income on which the whole university depends.

title: The Guardian view on schools: the hardest questions for Lucy Powell are about priorities | Editorial
summary:
The education secretary is right that her job is not to ‘polish the status quo’. Next, she must decide what to change first

There is a good case to be made for the increased importance of speaking skills in our new age of machines. With the UK economy’s stronger-than-expected recent performance widely linked to AI investment, it is vital that people are equipped for the kinds of in-person, public-facing jobs that are least likely to be automated. A concerning decline in children’s language development, both in the UK and internationally, has been linked to high screen use. There is a grim irony in a situation where tech companies both compete with humans for contracts and undermine our ability to talk to one other.

The Guardian has previously backed efforts to more strongly embed speaking skills, or oracy, in British schools. In a speech on Thursday, Lucy Powell promised to give them equal status to reading and writing in English (education is devolved, so her main responsibility is for England, but there are parallel initiatives in the other nations). Yet with promised updates to the national curriculum postponed, and plans for special educational needs reform causing deep anxiety to families, schools and councils, the hardest questions for the education secretary are about priorities. Following negative feedback from schools, she has also asked Ofsted to look again at its new inspection framework.

full_text:
There is a good case to be made for the increased importance of speaking skills in our new age of machines. With the UK economy’s stronger-than-expected recent performance widely linked to AI investment, it is vital that people are equipped for the kinds of in-person, public-facing jobs that are least likely to be automated. A concerning decline in children’s language development, both in the UK and internationally, has been linked to high screen use. There is a grim irony in a situation where tech companies both compete with humans for contracts and undermine our ability to talk to one other.

The Guardian has previously backed efforts to more strongly embed speaking skills, or oracy, in British schools. In a speech on Thursday, Lucy Powell promised to give them equal status to reading and writing in English (education is devolved, so her main responsibility is for England, but there are parallel initiatives in the other nations). Yet with promised updates to the national curriculum postponed, and plans for special educational needs reform causing deep anxiety to families, schools and councils, the hardest questions for the education secretary are about priorities. Following negative feedback from schools, she has also asked Ofsted to look again at its new inspection framework.

The curriculum review completed last year was deliberately cautious, reflecting the Starmer administration’s overall tone. Since then, England’s high scores in maths and science, in international tests, have shown that standards in some subjects have risen. But in English, an overly prescriptive and grammar-obsessed curriculum is putting pupils off. This is the obvious place to start with new speaking skills. The delayed curriculum revisions should set out how it is going to be done.

The energy that Ms Powell brings to the education brief is welcome. She is right to refuse to “sit still and polish the status quo”, especially as the Conservative party seeks to take credit for improvements to English schools that were a legacy of New Labour. The decline of the arts in schools must also be tackled. An improved vocational offer is arguably most urgent of all.

But there is no point denying the challenges around implementation. The government is already committed to the introduction of new maths and English qualifications, to replace demoralising GCSE resits. Reform of the special educational needs system will need to be carefully monitored. Many experts in the college sector believe that the scrapping of BTec qualifications, in favour of T-levels and V-levels, is a mistake. This too needs to be closely watched. A stronger steer from government on universities is also needed. Bridget Phillipson’s decision to unfreeze fees after eight years has only slightly eased their funding difficulties. Reform of unfair student loan terms must come sooner rather than later.

Ms Powell is not unique, among Andy Burnham’s new brooms, in facing a daunting set of challenges. Her pledge to go “further and deeper on curriculum reform” is welcome; the world is changing fast and schools need help to keep up. A strengthened emphasis on the spoken word is just one part of this. But in the coming months, she will need to make decisions about where to put her energies. There are only so many changes, on top of special educational needs reforms, that schools can be expected to cope with.

title: AI giant Anthropic commits 5% of shares to ‘public benefit’ fund
summary: Claude creator says fund could be used for donations to NGOs and 'direct distributions to specific populations'.
full_text:
Anthropic has pledged to commit 5 percent of its shares to a new fund dedicated to the public good, with plans to increase the contribution as the artificial intelligence giant’s market value grows.

The creator of the AI assistant Claude announced the new “Anthropic Public Benefit Fund” on Sunday as tech firms face intense scrutiny over the potential dangers posed by the frontier technology.

list 4 of 4Flight from Israel makes emergency landing in Bulgaria after bomb threat

end of list

In a blog post, Anthropic said it was committing 5 percent of company shares with immediate effect, subject to stockholder approval, with an additional 2 percent to be added “at the board’s discretion” for every 50 percent increase in the company’s value.

“Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good,” the San Francisco-based firm said.

“It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.”

Anthropic said the fund could be used to make donations to traditional nonprofits, as well as “direct distributions to specific populations”.

It said labour market disruption due to AI could be among the causes addressed by the fund.

“Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed,” the company said.

“The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”

Anthropic, officially registered as a “public benefit corporation” in the US state of Delaware, said the fund would not be used for lobbying or political donations, either in the United States or overseas.

Founded in 2021 by former employees of ChatGPT creator OpenAI, Anthropic is preparing for what could be the largest public initial offering in history. It is expected to list on the US stock market before the end of 2026, with analysts forecasting a valuation exceeding $2 trillion.

The company’s charter requires its leadership to balance shareholder returns with responsible AI development.

The breakneck speed of AI development has prompted widespread anxiety about possible negative downstream effects on society, including the job market.

In a report published last month, consulting firm McKinsey estimated that up to 11 million American workers may need to switch careers over the next decade due to AI-driven automation.

title: When an 89.4 Becomes a Crisis: Rethinking Precision in College Grading
summary:
The Decimal Point Problem During one of my first semesters teaching introductory biology labs at the college level, a student approached me after class visibly frustrated about a final grade. The difference between the student’s current average and the next letter grade was less than one percentage point. What struck me was not the disappointment […]

The post When an 89.4 Becomes a Crisis: Rethinking Precision in College Grading appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
The Decimal Point Problem

During one of my first semesters teaching introductory biology labs at the college level, a student approached me after class visibly frustrated about a final grade. The difference between the student’s current average and the next letter grade was less than one percentage point. What struck me was not the disappointment itself, but how narrowly the conversation focused on decimals rather than learning. The student was not asking what concepts still needed improvement, which scientific skills needed development, or how to strengthen understanding moving forward. The discussion centered almost entirely on points.

Over time, I began noticing how frequently grading conversations in higher education become negotiations over mathematical precision. Students monitor learning management systems constantly, calculate hypothetical grade combinations, and focus intensely on small numerical differences that may not meaningfully represent actual differences in understanding. In many classrooms, grading can unintentionally shift attention away from learning and toward point accumulation.

This experience has made me reconsider how percentage-based grading systems shape student behavior in college courses.

When Students Chase Points Instead of Learning

American higher education relies heavily on highly granular grading systems. A student may earn an 89.4, a 91.7, or a 93.2, and those distinctions often carry emotional and academic significance. Yet as instructors, we should ask whether these fine numerical differences always represent truly distinct levels of mastery. In practice, many assessments contain unavoidable subjectivity, especially in written responses, projects, participation, discussion quality, or open-ended scientific reasoning tasks.

In contrast, many international grading models rely on broader performance bands such as 1–5 scales or competency-based descriptors. While these systems vary significantly across countries and institutions, they often place greater emphasis on overall mastery categories rather than hyper-precise numerical distinctions. The question is not whether one system is universally superior. Rather, the comparison raises an important instructional issue: How much grading precision is genuinely meaningful for student learning?

In my own courses, I have observed that highly detailed percentage systems can sometimes encourage transactional learning behaviors. Students may become preoccupied with recovering partial credit, calculating minimum scores needed for target grades, or strategically allocating effort based on point values rather than intellectual engagement. This does not mean students are unmotivated. In many cases, they are responding rationally to systems that reward optimization and numerical performance tracking.

At the same time, highly granular grading may unintentionally increase anxiety for students already navigating demanding academic workloads. Small numerical fluctuations can feel disproportionately important when students perceive every decimal point as carrying major consequences. In introductory STEM courses especially, where students may already experience high levels of performance pressure, grading structures can significantly shape classroom climate and motivation.

This does not necessarily mean instructors should eliminate percentage grades entirely. Many institutions require them, and numerical grading can provide useful feedback in certain contexts. However, college faculty can still take practical steps to reduce unhealthy fixation on points while keeping assessment rigorous and transparent.

As someone currently pursuing a doctoral degree while also teaching at both the secondary and postsecondary levels, I have found myself reflecting on grading from the student perspective as well. In several doctoral courses, I have received assignment grades reported with highly specific percentages even when the accompanying rubric used only whole-number performance categories. At times, this creates confusion about what the decimal-level distinctions are actually measuring. If a rubric category distinguishes performance broadly between levels such as “proficient” and “advanced,” the addition of highly granular percentages can give the impression of mathematical precision that may not fully align with the inherently interpretive nature of evaluating complex academic writing and analysis. More importantly, it can shift student attention toward trying to decode tiny numerical differences rather than focusing on substantive feedback, revision, and intellectual growth. As both an instructor and current student, these experiences have increasingly made me question whether highly detailed grading always improves clarity or whether it sometimes unintentionally amplifies anxiety and performance fixation instead.

Rethinking Feedback and Precision

One useful strategy involves shifting feedback emphasis toward mastery and growth rather than numerical outcomes alone. For example, when returning laboratory reports or written assignments, instructors can prioritize comments explaining conceptual strengths, scientific reasoning, and areas for improvement before students immediately focus on scores. Rubrics can also emphasize broader competency categories such as evidence use, analytical reasoning, communication clarity, or methodological understanding rather than excessively fragmented point breakdowns.

Another helpful approach is reducing unnecessary grading precision when appropriate. In some assignments, broader scoring bands may better reflect authentic performance differences than extremely narrow numerical distinctions. For example, distinguishing between “excellent,” “proficient,” “developing,” and “limited” scientific explanations may communicate learning quality more effectively than assigning a score of 87 versus 89.

Beyond Mathematical Accuracy

Transparency also matters. Students benefit when instructors explicitly explain what grades are intended to represent. Are grades measuring compliance, effort, conceptual understanding, skill development, improvement over time, or performance on isolated assessments? Many student frustrations emerge not simply from grades themselves, but from uncertainty about what those grades actually communicate.

I have also found that conversations about grading become more productive when students are encouraged to reflect on learning behaviors instead of solely final outcomes. Questions such as “What study strategies worked?” or “At what point did confusion begin?” often lead to more meaningful academic discussions than conversations focused entirely on whether one additional point can be recovered.

Grading systems shape more than transcripts. They influence motivation, classroom culture, student identity, and how learners define academic success. As higher education continues discussing student engagement, mental health, and authentic learning, grading practices deserve closer examination as part of that broader conversation. The goal is not to make courses easier or reduce standards. Rather, it is to consider whether our grading systems consistently direct student attention toward the forms of learning we actually value most.

Christopher Morales is a high school science teacher in Southwest Florida and an adjunct professor of biology at Florida SouthWestern State College. He holds both a bachelor’s and master’s degree in biology and is currently pursuing a doctorate in Educational Leadership at the American College of Education. His work focuses on student attention, learning environments, engagement, and instructional practice across secondary and postsecondary education.

title: Community-Guided Teaching: Building Relationships Before Course Design
summary:
A Relational Framework for Community-Guided Teaching in Higher Education  In higher education, many instructors want to include Indigenous perspectives, experiential learning, and community-engaged approaches in their courses, but they are not always sure how to begin. Yet the question is not only whether this work should be done, but how it should be done. Without […]

The post Community-Guided Teaching: Building Relationships Before Course Design appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
A Relational Framework for Community-Guided Teaching in Higher Education

In higher education, many instructors want to include Indigenous perspectives, experiential learning, and community-engaged approaches in their courses, but they are not always sure how to begin. Yet the question is not only whether this work should be done, but how it should be done. Without ongoing consultation with Indigenous community partners, Indigenous content can be added symbolically rather than relationally. University timelines can also pressure educators to move quickly toward course outcomes before trust and community guidance have had time to develop.

This article grew out of a collaboration between Safieh Moghaddam, a non-Indigenous professor at the University of Toronto Scarborough; Carol Ducharme, an Indigenous colleague and Assistant Director of the Indigenous Initiatives Office; and Elders from Curve Lake First Nation, whose guidance shaped the work. Through this process, the authors learned that meaningful engagement develops slowly through listening, trust, community guidance and a willingness to let relationships shape the direction of teaching.

A critical consideration before beginning this work was Safieh’s recognition, as a non-Indigenous educator, that good intentions were not enough. She understood the importance of approaching the work with humility and positioning herself as a learner rather than an expert. This required a shift away from the usual role of professor. Instead of leading, planning, and deciding from the outset, she had to slow down and allow the work to be shaped by community relationships. This required courage: the courage to step back and accept that meaningful community-guided teaching begins with learning from others.

This article introduces the Relationship Before Research (RBR) Framework, a reflective approach that emerged through our collaboration with Curve Lake First Nation and later shaped our teaching practices. Rather than beginning with a finalized syllabus, planned experiential learning activity, or course plan, the framework emphasizes community direction, relational accountability, and reciprocity. We do not present the RBR Framework as a universal blueprint or rigid formula. Instead, it offers educators a practical starting point for approaching Indigenous-informed and community-engaged teaching with greater care, patience, and ethical responsibility. Four interconnected phases became central to the teaching adaptation of the framework: listening and relational foundation-building, community guidance and ethical practice, pedagogical integration, and reciprocity and sustainability.

Figure 1 – The Relationship Before Research (RBR) Framework as Applied to Teaching.

Although presented as separate phases, they often overlap and evolve throughout the teaching process.

Phase 1: Listening and Building a Relational Foundation

Safieh’s first instinct was to approach the project the way many academics are trained to: start with a course plan, define learning outcomes, and organize activities for the semester. However, after consultation with Carol Ducharme and collaboration with Elders from Curve Lake First Nation, it became clear that a different approach was needed. This required slowing down, listening carefully, and allowing relationships to guide the process.

In this first phase, conversations with Elders focused on community priorities, respectful engagement, ethical responsibilities, and what meaningful collaboration might look like in a teaching context. Rather than immediately organizing guest lectures or experiential learning activities, the early stages centred on trust and reciprocity. This reflected Wilson’s (2008) concept of relational accountability, where teaching is shaped by responsibilities to the relationships that make it possible.

This phase also reinforced the importance of students learning directly from Elders and community members as well as through guided experiences. Rather than positioning the instructor as the primary authority on Indigenous knowledge, the work emphasized humility, relational learning, and shared guidance.

As trust developed, Elder and community input began to shape decisions about classroom integration, student preparation, reflective activities, journaling, and appropriate ways to introduce Indigenous-informed learning into undergraduate courses. This highlighted the importance of consultation before implementation and relationships before course design.

Phase 2: Community Guidance, Teaching Integration, and Ethical Practice

Consultation could not happen only once at the beginning of the collaboration. As the partnership with Curve Lake First Nation continued to grow, ongoing conversations with Elders and community members remained central to decisions about teaching activities, experiential learning opportunities, and classroom engagement.

Elder and community guidance helped shape the integration of Indigenous-informed learning into undergraduate linguistics courses, including guest lectures, land-based learning opportunities, reflective activities, journaling, and classroom discussions. These were not treated as isolated course additions. Instead, this phase emphasized reciprocity, adaptability, and relational learning. The instructor’s role was not to interpret or represent Indigenous knowledge, but to listen, reflect, and learn under the guidance of Elders and the community.

Questions of ethical responsibility also became increasingly important, including student preparation, classroom reflection, and how community knowledge should be discussed and represented in teaching spaces. The work was informed by OCAP® principles, particularly around consent, accountability, and respectful engagement.

This phase also highlighted the need for responsiveness in community-guided teaching. Rather than relying only on standard university structures or predetermined classroom plans, teaching activities continued to evolve through community input.

Phase 3: Pedagogical Integration

In the classroom, the work invited students to approach language as more than course content. In Safieh’s undergraduate sociolinguistics courses, Elder-led teachings, reflective journaling, classroom discussions, and land-based learning helped students consider language in relation to social life, land, history, oral tradition, identity, relationships, and community knowledge. This approach aligns with Jo-Ann Archibald’s (2008) Indigenous Storywork principles, including respect, responsibility, reciprocity, reverence, holism, and interconnectedness.

One of the most meaningful components was a full-day land-based visit to Curve Lake First Nation, where students spent the day with Elders. They received teachings from Elders who carry this knowledge through lived experience, rather than learning only through abstract concepts or textbook material. The visit invited students to think about language, culture, and knowledge in more relational and land-based ways. Rather than positioning students as passive observers, it emphasized active engagement, responsibility, and community guidance.

This phase also reinforced the importance of careful preparation before community-engaged learning. Before the visit, students participated in discussions and reflective activities focused on positionality, respectful engagement, community protocols, and the historical impacts of colonial education. This helped them enter the space with greater humility, respect, and awareness.

Following the visit, reflection remained central throughout the process. Through journaling, written responses, and discussions connected to Elder teachings and the land-based learning experience, students were encouraged to think critically about language, relationships, community, and accountability. These activities helped them connect course concepts to lived experience in more meaningful ways.

Student reflections suggested that the visit felt different from learning abstract concepts in a classroom. Several students noted that they were not only learning about language, culture, and history, but receiving these teachings from Elders who had lived these experiences and generously shared their knowledge.

For some students, the visit was also deeply moving and healing. It created a stronger sense of connection, respect, and responsibility and helped them understand that learning in this context is not only intellectual, but also relational and ethical.

What This Looked Like in Practice

In practice, this approach included Elder-led guest lectures, classroom discussions, journaling, and a land-based visit to Curve Lake First Nation. Students prepared beforehand through discussions of respectful engagement, positionality, colonial histories, and local protocols. After the visit, they participated in guided discussions and written reflections about language, relationships, accountability, and experiential learning.

Phase 4: Reciprocity and Sustainability

One of the most important lessons from this work is that community-engaged teaching cannot end when a course or semester finishes. Within the RBR Framework, reciprocity means considering how teaching practices and experiential learning can support long-term community priorities. In the Curve Lake collaboration, this meant continuing conversations about how the teaching could evolve in respectful and sustainable ways. Rather than treating Indigenous-informed teaching as a one-time activity or isolated guest lecture, the emphasis remained on accountability, consultation, and long-term collaboration.

Sustainability also involved encouraging students to engage with community-created educational materials, journaling, and discussions that connected classroom learning to broader histories and responsibilities. Ultimately, sustainability is not simply about repeating an activity in a future course. It is about continuing dialogue and remaining accountable to the people and communities who make this teaching possible.

Reflections and Practical Challenges

Implementing community-guided teaching in higher education can be deeply meaningful, but it requires patience, flexibility, and reflection. One challenge is balancing institutional timelines with relational ones. Universities operate through semesters, course schedules, assignment deadlines, and curriculum planning, while relationships develop gradually through trust and continued presence. Educators may therefore need to slow down and avoid moving activities forward before guidance is fully established.

Another important consideration involves reconsidering the instructor’s role. In community-guided teaching, the instructor is not the primary knowledge holder or decision-maker. This requires careful listening, openness to guidance, and recognition of community expertise. For many educators, this means moving away from instructor-centred approaches and creating opportunities for students to learn from Elders and community members.

Accountability must also be part of teaching practice itself. Community-engaged learning should not become symbolic, temporary, or disconnected from community priorities. Educators need to consider how Indigenous knowledge is represented in the classroom, who benefits from the learning experience, and whether relationships continue beyond a single guest lecture, classroom visit, or experiential activity.

Recommendations for Educators

For educators interested in community-guided teaching, the RBR Framework offers several practical starting points. Relationship-building should begin before developing a syllabus, experiential learning activity, guest lecture, or assignment. Meaningful engagement takes time and cannot be rushed to fit semester timelines.

Consultation should continue throughout the process, since community priorities, concerns, and availability may shift. This work also benefits from institutional support, including teaching and learning centres, experiential learning offices, Indigenous initiatives offices, libraries, and administrative partners.

Student preparation is equally important. Before community-engaged learning, students need space to reflect on positionality, colonial histories, respectful engagement, and local protocols. Journaling, discussion, and classroom preparation can help them enter these learning spaces with humility and responsibility.

Finally, instructors need to remain responsive. Community-guided teaching cannot always follow a rigid syllabus or predetermined plan. Elder availability, evolving relationships, and community priorities are central to ethical teaching practice.

Conclusion

Integrating Indigenous perspectives into higher education teaching is not simply a matter of adding content to a syllabus. It requires attention to relationships, responsibilities, community priorities, and guidance. The RBR Framework encourages educators to slow down, listen carefully, and build community-engaged teaching through reciprocity and sustained collaboration. By prioritizing relationships over course design, classroom implementation, and institutional timelines, educators can move beyond symbolic inclusion toward more meaningful teaching and learning.

Carol Ducharme is a Saulteaux community member of Keeseekoose First Nation. She has an interdisciplinary background in Dental Hygiene, Adult Education, Indigenous Education, Indigenous pedagogies, and curriculum integration. Her work is grounded in relational values, lived experience, and the Indigenous perspectives and teachings received through relationships with Elders, Knowledge Keepers, communities, and learners. Her experience spans across post-secondary education, Indigenous community engagement, faculty development, and project management. She currently works in the Indigenous Initiatives Office at the University of Toronto Scarborough.

She holds a Master of Education (Post-Secondary Studies), a Bachelor of Education (Aboriginal Adult Education), and a Diploma in Dental Hygiene, along with additional training in health, mental health, and trauma-informed approaches. In her university-facing work, she supports faculty in integrating Indigenous perspectives, knowledge, and pedagogies into curriculum, teaching practice, and student learning experiences.

Sharing knowledge and responsibilities is a central motivator in her work. She supports learning spaces where Indigenous knowledge is approached with humility, accountability, respect, and reciprocity. In a previous role as Assistant Director of Indigenous Initiatives at the University of Toronto, she supported reconciliation-focused initiatives, Indigenous programming, and a community language revitalization project with Curve Lake First Nation.

Dr. Safieh Moghaddam (PhD, University of Toronto) is an Associate Professor (Teaching Stream) of Linguistics in the Department of Language Studies at the University of Toronto Scarborough (UTSC). Her research concentrates on sociolinguistics (the interaction of language, culture, gender, and race/ethnicity), linguistic typology and universals (the documentation of minority and endangered languages, as well as the syntax and morphology of endangered and less-studied languages). In the classroom, she focuses on active and cooperative learning and on course design for hybrid (dual delivery) and fully online formats. She has developed and redesigned undergraduate courses at all levels, aligning assessments with clear learning outcomes and creating learner-centered syllabi and activities. Her teaching approach emphasizes consistent, actionable feedback and strong student-instructor relationships to foster engagement, equity, and student success.
